title: What is known about 1RB0LA_0RC0RB_1LD1LA_1LC1RE_1RF0RD_1LC---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LA_0RC0RB_1LD1LA_1LC1RE_1RF0RD_1LC---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open; probviously halting, astronomically late. At each E-pass the run is a pair (context word c, block length n): n → (3n+δ)/2 and c → c', decided by c and n mod 4. The arithmetic is now derived from the machine and proved in Lean for every context and every n; the context is rewritten like a binary counter read from the right. Two rules halt (11111 and 1111011 with ⌈n/2⌉ odd; proved). The bits ⌈n/2⌉ mod 2 are provably uniform over residues of n, so halting has a fixed rate of 8.9·10−13 per pass: a halt is expected after about 1.1·1012 passes. No halt in the first 4.3·109 passes (218 of them proved in Lean, more than 1045000 steps).

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: The E-pass for every context
claims.text: For every left tape P and every n: P E> 1^n reaches P C> 1^(3k+2) (k = ⌈n/2⌉ even) or P 1 C> 1^(3k+2) (k odd): the block is halved into (01)^k and every two 01 become six 1s. The arithmetic of the map does not depend on the context.

claims.title: The context rewrites of the 55 contexts the orbit uses
claims.text: For each context met in the first 230 passes and each bit b, the rewrite c C> 1^m → c' E> 1^(m+a) for every block length m of the right parity: 110 rules, generated with symtm.

claims.title: The map, for every n
claims.text: nextE_sound: from the E-event (c, n), n ≥ 6, c in the table, the machine reaches the E-event the map predicts, n' = (3n+δ)/2. From blank tape the first E-event is (1, 19) at step 153.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>1700</sup> steps
claims.text: 10,000 passes of the map from (1, 19) stay inside the proved table, evaluated by the kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>45000</sup> steps
claims.text: 218 = 262,144 passes by native_decide (222 also check, in 29 minutes, not in check.sh).

claims.title: The halting criterion
claims.text: If the orbit reaches the context 11111 or 1111011 with ⌈n/2⌉ odd, the machine halts; if it stays in the table forever, it never halts. These two rules carry all but 10−16 of the halting rate of the Markov model.

claims.title: No halt in the first 4.3·10<sup>9</sup> passes
claims.text: c/orbit.c iterates the map 232 times by divide and conquer on the low bits of n (n_k = (3kn + B_k)/2k, GMP), 18 minutes; 65 contexts, none longer than 11 cells; n ends with 2.5·109 bits. Checked against plain big-integer iteration for 220 passes.

claims.title: Probviously halting, after about 10<sup>12</sup> passes
claims.text: The bits ⌈n/2⌉ mod 2 of the next k passes are a bijective image of n mod 2<sup>k+1</sup> for every context, so they are fresh fair bits whatever the size of n. The context is then a Markov chain with absorption rate 8.87·10<sup>−13</sup> per pass (mean 1.1·10<sup>12</sup> passes); its stationary distribution matches the orbit's context frequencies to four digits. A halt in the 4.3·10<sup>9</sup> passes checked had probability 0.4 %.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. A halt is expected after about 10<sup>12</sup> passes, i.e. some 10<sup>7·10<sup>10</sup></sup> steps; deciding it needs control of the parity sequence of a 3/2-Collatz orbit.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RF_1LC---_1LF1LD_1RE0LD_0RC0RE_1LC1RA up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Probably yes, but so late that no computer could ever watch it. The machine multiplies a number n by about 3/2 again and again; a short word on the far left of the tape is updated after every pass like a binary counter, steered by one bit of n per pass. Two values of that word make the machine stop. Those bits behave like coin flips, and the coins would land right about once in a trillion passes.

facts.text: No halt in the first 2<sup>32</sup> passes from blank tape (n then has 2.5 billion bits).
Mean time to a halt: the halting rate is a fixed 8.9·10<sup>−13</sup> per pass.
No halt, proved by Lean's kernel (10<sup>45000</sup> with native_decide), via the proved map.

sections.heading: A 3/2 map and a word that counts
html: Look at the moments when the head, in state E, steps from the left onto the last run of 1s on the tape. The tape is then a short word c (the context) followed by a block of n ones:

<svg viewBox="0 0 560 110" role="img" aria-label="the tape at an E-event" style="width:100%;max-width:560px;height:auto;font:12px var(--mono);">
<rect x="10" y="40" width="90" height="30" fill="var(--accent)" fill-opacity=".18" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="55" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">c = 10001</text>
<rect x="100" y="40" width="400" height="30" fill="none" stroke="var(--line)"/><text x="300" y="60" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fg2)">1^n</text>
<polygon points="100,28 94,18 106,18" fill="var(--head)"/><text x="112" y="24" fill="var(--head)">E</text>
<text x="55" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">context</text><text x="300" y="95" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--muted)">block, n → (3n+δ)/2</text>
</svg>

One pass does three things. Halve: the head runs right through the block turning 11 into 01, so 1^n becomes (01)^k with k = ⌈n/2⌉. Triple: working leftwards, every two 01 are erased and the block at the right end grows by six cells, so a block of 3k + 2 ones is rebuilt (if k is odd, the last 01 leaves an extra 1 on the context). Count: the head then reaches the context, and state A adds one to it as a binary number (A turns trailing 1s into 0s and the first 0 into a 1, exactly like adding 1 by hand); depending on what it finds there it feeds a bit of the context into the block or starts the next pass.

The halving and tripling are the same for every context, and Lean checks them for every n. Altogether n becomes (3n + δ)/2, where δ is a small number set by the context, and the context changes according to one bit b = ⌈n/2⌉ mod 2:

From blank tape: (1, 19) → (11, 37) → (10001, 61) → (11, 103) → (1, 163) → (11, 253) → … With bits 0, 1, 0, 1, … the context counts upwards (1, 10001, 110001, 10000001, 10010001, 10110001, …); other bit pairs send it back. It is not a finite-state counter: the number of contexts reachable with some bit sequence grows exponentially with their length.

sections.heading: Yes, if the counter reads 11111 at the wrong moment
html: The machine stops when the counting step starts a pass on an inner run of 1s that is followed by 0 1: state F then reads a 1, which has no instruction. That happens for exactly two contexts that matter, 11111 and 1111011, when the bit is 1. Lean proves that reaching either one halts the machine.

Getting there takes luck: the quickest route from 1 is 42 passes with one particular bit sequence (count up to 10110110001 without a mistake, then take a specific exit). The bits come from n itself, but they are as good as coin flips: the next k bits are fixed by the last k+1 binary digits of n, and every pattern of k bits belongs to exactly the same number of possible endings. The size of n never matters, because every pass uses a binary digit of the starting number that no earlier pass used.

With fair coins the context wanders among a few hundred short words. Its long-run frequencies match the real run to four digits (the word 1 appears 34.57 % of the time in both), and it falls into a halting rule with probability 8.9·10−13 per pass: a halt is expected after about a trillion passes. Each pass multiplies n by 1.5, so by then n would have some 250 billion binary digits, and the step count about 1070,000,000,000.

The run from blank tape has been followed for 4.3 billion passes (with a divide-and-conquer trick on the low bits of n, in 18 minutes) without a halt, as expected: the chance of an earlier halt was 0.4 %. Among the bbchallenge holdouts most cryptids are expected never to halt; this one is expected to halt, absurdly late.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.049). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.497).
After 109 steps the tape spans 63,226 cells (25 left of the start, 45,537 right), with a density of 1s of 0.331.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: 3/2-Collatz n -> (3n+d)/2 (proved in Lean for every n) driven by a binary-counter-like context word; two rules halt (proved); the bits are provably fair, so a halt is expected after ~10^12 passes (probviously halting); no halt in 4.3e9 passes.
family: 3/2 Collatz with a binary-counter context word (probviously halting, very late)
